title: Why does Kendall have a hard time choosing between killing Logan and worshipping him? (Succession)

commenti.body:
You're over thinking and interpreting way too much into a TV show that is nothing more than a well acted soap similar in plot to something like The Young and the Restless.

It was a personal struggle for me to finish the series. Things happen because they happen, there's not much of a motive behind actions other that the typical reason of "he wants to be out of his father's shadow". Nothing deep or remotely interesting about that. We've seen it a billion times before.

A soap?  A tv show that's basically people talking to each other in closed spaces and sometimes open spaces mostly shot on handheld camera with shots that look like gonzo documentary felt like a soap to you? Not counting the copious amounts of scenes where characters literally explain their or other characters motives and intentions, countless other narrative elements that imply the characters intentions and a whole writing style that's entirely evolved to convey subtext ( words are just complicated air flow), you couldn't piece together the characters motivations and psyche from the exceptional perfomance of the cast and the emotions they portray? I'm lost.

You've just described a soap, or a telenovela as they say. Yes, it's shot better. It has better writing, though that isn't much for a soap. It is well acted, I've mentioned that from the start, but at it's core, it is a classic telenovela that is taken up a notch. But I still feel unimpressed with the very basic premise that we've seen oh so many times before. Nice execution? Sure, but still lackluster as a whole.

Spoilers:
Well as with much of the show, it’s incredibly complicated. I mean all of Logan’s children, and even his colleagues have incredibly complicated feelings about him, even his oldest “friends” like Geri and Frank cant honestly say they miss him when he’s gone. Due to Logan’s immense power and influence over his children’s lives, because of the intersecting and contradictory dichotomy of him being both their “loving and guiding” paternal figure and their competition, they are constantly in uneasy territory, uncertain whether their lives as his children surpass his own desire for power. Even though materially they have been given everything, each one of them has a gigantic hole that is constantly waiting to be filled. Because their family dynamic is really no different than a corporate one, built on capitalistic competition and political moves, strangely enough hostility takes the place of love and fulfills the same urge. Kendall can only win his fathers approval by mercilessly deposing him, because he’s been convinced that Logan only values strength, and has very little reason to think otherwise by seeing how Logan treats those who he’s most intimately acquainted, such as wives and old friends. But tragically and amusingly, Logan is both impressed and disappointed at the same time, leading to a furthering of this dynamic that is self destructive and contradictory. He’s impressed that his son has the same drive for self sustenance and drive for power, but he’s also hurt that his own son would be so hostile to him at the same time, and disappointed that Kendall hasn’t already beaten him yet. What you see in the final season of the show is Logan realizing that all the family turmoil and venomous feuding that we saw in the earlier season was entirely his fault. It was due to the promise of succession and the intertwining with business and family that destroyed their stability and that holding the crown for all his children to see and try to acquire would do nothing but destroy them. But Kendall, by seeing his father define himself by his own position of power, began to define himself in the same terms, for him to self actualize he would need to prove to himself, his father and the whole world that he was his fathers equal. If Kendall wasn’t trying to take control of Waystar away from his father, there would have been no need for Logan to hold the caterers death over his head and threaten him with exposure. But as Logan’s child, Kendall feels in that moment progressively that in order to survive he must do what he says, not just to avoid prison, but also for the hope of reconciliation with his father, his most central relationship that has been strained. Kendall does extremely well, he does everything correct, he does exceptionally well in the congressional hearings but once it becomes politically convenient for Logan he decides to sacrifice Kendall for crimes that he himself is responsible. Kendall felt disposable as well as a disappointment, when Logan says that he wasn’t brutal enough for the top job.
Well name a few other shows with the same premise that you were impressed by, if any. I would like to know.
Wow. I'm curious to know your favourite show.

Interesting. Logan has a twisted sense of loyalty and there's no better example than the smirk he gives when Kendall does a 180 in S2 finale. 

(Also it was very difficult to read. Try putting your comment on bullet points or something)
The premise being family disputes and heirs to business empires and so on? Nothing comes to mind to be honest, I only know of Yellowstone. Bugt that is much, much worse.

I don't have favourites. Not in films, not in tv shows, not in music. I have been impressed by some more classical shows like The Sopranos for instance, or Band of Brothers. Or the early Twin Peaks for the atmosphere. More recent stuff, not so much. Mr Robot comes to mine, it had great storytelling techniques, though clearly not a perfect show. The british Sherlock also went in some weird artistic direction later on, and I enjoyed it.

To be honest it seemed like it was just another way for them to extend the series and milk it for 4 seasons. The plot of this show was extremely thin, it was basically just a revolving door of arbitrary betrayals and makeups. And then constant fakeouts on whether deals would go through and the company would go down or not.


IIRC he just had a change of heart in that moment because he thought it was unfair, or you could say it was his "inner Logan" coming out.
“I don’t have favorites, but here are some shows I like more than others, which I would just call my favorites if I wasn’t such a boring asshole.”
But Sopranos also has the family dynamic, if we consider Tony's Mafia as his family. And it's the greatest TV drama ever. But do you think it's wise to call drama as soap?

Agreed on all counts. They may have been able to make a great one-season miniseries out of the Roy family’s succession drama, weaving together a story about backstabbing cutthroat business politics and intense personal loss, but they seemed to be more interested in trying to maintain some long-term Game of Thrones-style drama about shifting factions and they just didn’t have the material.

Plus, everything is urgent *for a season*, as everyone is up in arms about Deal X or whatever, but then the outcome almost never seems to actually matter. Everyone’s living in their penthouse the next episode and talking about Merger Y. If they’d leaned into the characters’ invincibility born from Fuck You Money, maybe by showing how the consequences always fell on some poor schmuck or actual good person, there could be some satire and meaning. But the show refused to ever do anything more than worship the Roys.

I don’t think they’re saying that all drama or all family drama is soap, but that they don’t think Succession handled that drama much better than a soap opera. 

And I’m inclined to agree, in parts. Individual relationships seemed to be well-written, such as Tom and Shiv’s, which grows into something very interesting, but the main plotlines got very soap-ish IMO.

Do they have to be TV shows? Because I’d say The Godfather is a fantastic example of using the same or similar themes to *great* effect, and even extending the story to a sequel without being repetitive or reductive.
